Examination of preserved specimens from trawl surveys along the continental shelf of the northern South China Sea has provided detailed life-history information for the big-head pennah croaker Pennahia macrocephalus. Maximum longevity in this sciaenid, estimated from otolith readings of the oldest individuals captured, is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a figure that situates the species among the longer-lived member at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]s of its genus. All measurements and experimental observations reported here were conducted at a stable water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], reflecting the average bottom temperature of the species' primary habitat during the peak growing season. Under these conditions, the embryonic period is relatively brief: hatching occurs just 18 days [ab = 18 days] after fertilization, producing a tiny free-swimming larva at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females has been recorded at approximately 5% [GSI = approximately 5%] at a water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C].

Field sampling data indicate that puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, is attained when individuals reach a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. This length-at-puberty is a critical demographic parameter because it marks the transition from the juvenile growth phase to the period during which energetic resources are increasingly directed toward gamete production rather than somatic expansion. Corresponding to this length threshold, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 48.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 48.5 grams], a body mass that represents a substantial fraction of the species' maximum adult size. The body weight of individuals at the point of hatching is negligible in comparison: ichthyoplankton surveys combined with laboratory rearing experiments have estimated the wet weight at birth to be 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], derived from the average egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter. This extremely small neonatal mass reflects the pelagic, free-spawning reproductive mode typical of sciaenids, in which females release large numbers of small, buoyant eggs into the water column.

Growth trajectories reconstructed from length-at-age data indicate that the ultimate total length achieved by Pennahia macrocephalus under natural conditions is 27.8 centimeters [Li = 27.8 centimeters]. This asymptotic length appears to be reached relatively early in the lifespan, a pattern consistent with the rapid early growth phase documented in other tropical croaker species. In terms of corresponding body mass, the ultimate wet weight of adult individuals has been estimated at 412.4 grams [Wwi = 412.4 grams], a value derived from published length-weight relationships for this species. There exists a pronounced allometric relationship between length and weight, such that the transition from the pubertal length of 14 centimeters to the asymptotic length of nearly 28 centimeters is accompanied by nearly an order of magnitude increase in mass. This steep growth curve in the sub-adult phase likely reflects an interval of intensive feeding prior to the full onset of reproductive investment, a common pattern among iteroparous marine teleosts.

The reproductive biology of Pennahia macrocephalus reflects a strategy typical of many temperate and subtropical sciaenids, with a protracted spawning season coinciding with warmer water temperatures. Females are batch spawners, releasing multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over the course of several months. Reported values from histological analyses of ovarian tissue indicate that individual females produce approximately 150,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 150,000 eggs per clutch], with the potential to spawn roughly 30 clutches per year [F_R_i = roughly 30 clutches per year]. The high fecundity at each spawning event, combined with the extended spawning period, results in a substantial annual reproductive output that compensates for the high rates of egg and larval mortality characteristic of pelagic early life stages. This bet-hedging reproductive strategy, wherein reproductive effort is distributed across many small batches, is common among marine fishes that inhabit unpredictable environments, as it spreads the risk of total reproductive failure across the entire season.

From a comparative life-history perspective, the biological parameters of the big-head pennah croaker place it firmly within the slow end of the fast-slow continuum for sciaenid fishes of comparable body size. Individuals regularly survive for more than a decade and a half (15 years) [am = 15 years] at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a longevity that is notably high for a warm-water species and suggests a relatively low rate of physiological aging. This extended lifespan is complemented by a moderate age at first reproduction, corresponding to the attainment of the pubertal length of 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm]; individuals typically reach this size during their second year of life. The wide disparity between the minute hatchling mass of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] and the adult wet weight at puberty of 48.5 grams [Wwp = 48.5 grams] underscores the enormous scope for post-hatching growth that characterizes this species. Adult individuals ultimately plateau at an asymptotic mass of 412.4 grams [Wwi = 412.4 grams] and a corresponding total length of 27.8 cm [Li = 27.8 cm], representing the physical constraint imposed by the species' morphology and ecological niche.
